Learning Objectives
Review the patient history, patient presentation, physical examination findings, and imaging
studies consistent with lateral elbow instability.
Describe the pathophysiology and natural history of lateral collateral ligament insufficiency of
the elbow.
Demonstrate an understanding of the management of varus and posterior rotatory instability
of the elbow.

Overview

Elbow instability caused by disruption or insufficiency of the lateral elbow collateral ligament
complex, primarily lateral ulnar collateral ligament (LUCL)
Usually associated with traumatic dislocation or varus stress/external rotation moment
Posterolateral Rotatory Instability
Posterolateral rotatory instability (PLRI) may occur after elbow dislocation, iatrogenically or in a
delayed fashion after varus malunion of the distal humerus (cubitus varus).1-3
Insufficiency of the LUCL is the essential lesion.4,5
Concomitant deficiencies in the coronoid, radial head, and medial collateral ligament (MCL)
can further destabilize the elbow.
Epidemiology
The highest incidence of elbow dislocation is in patients aged 10 to 20 years.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology

Osteology
The elbow is one of the most congruous joints of the musculoskeletal system, which
imparts great osseous stability, especially in higher flexion angles. The distal humeral
articulation is forward flexed 30°, which is matched with a 30° posterior orientation of
the greater sigmoid notch of the proximal ulna. Therefore, elbow joint motion occurs
about a hinge axis through the center of the capitellum and trochlea. Varus stress is
resisted primarily by the distal half or coronoid portion of the greater sigmoid notch,
both in extension (67%) and in flexion (60%).6,7
Tendons

Tendons

Varus stress is checked nearly equally in extension by the bony joint articulations and
the soft-tissue restraints; however, in flexion, the osseous articulations provide 75% of
the varus stability.
Ligaments and Biomechanics
Lateral collateral ligament complex (LCLC): blend of fibers with loosely defined borders4,8
Although separate bands are defined based on their distal insertions, these bands largely
share a common origin on the humerus. The humeral origin is the most common site of
rupture and, therefore, these bands are most commonly torn in tandem.
LUCL
Primary static stabilizer to varus external rotation stress at the elbow
Origin: lateral humeral epicondyle, 10.7 mm distal9
Insertion: tubercle of the supinator crest of ulna, 3.3 mm distal to the apex of the supinator
crest9
Isolated section of the ulnar insertion of the LUCL: does not result in gross instability4
Lateral radial collateral ligament (RCL)
Origin: anterior to the LUCL on the lateral epicondyle
Insertion: blends with the annular ligament fibers
Computational models show combined LUCL and lateral RCL ruptures are associated with
considerably greater instability than isolated LUCL lesions.10
Accessory lateral collateral ligament (LCL)
Origin: annular ligament
Insertion: supinator crest of the ulna
Annular ligament
Tethers ulna and radius, maintains radioulnar articulation
LCLs—The LUCL and the RCL prevent rotational subluxation of the forearm away from the
humerus. The LUCL and lateral RCL must be compromised for the lateral ligaments to
become insufficient
The radial head plays a role in posterolateral rotatory stability by tensioning the LUCL and
acting as a secondary buttress against posterior subluxation of the forearm relative to the
humerus if the coronoid is fractured in patients with a terrible triad injury.
Radial head/neck fractures may act as functional ruptures of the LUCL.

Secondary static constraints to elbow
Capsule (most stabilizing effect with elbow extended)
Radiocapitellar articulation (important secondary valgus stabilizer)
Ulnohumeral articulation
Coronoid (restraint to posterior elbow dislocation)
Common flexor and extensor tendon origins
Dynamic constraints to elbow
Dynamic constraint is provided by the muscles that cross the elbow joint (the anconeus,
triceps, and brachialis).
These muscles apply compressive force.
Etiology
Mechanisms of injury for posterolateral dislocations
The classic mechanism of injury is thought to be a combination of axial loading, external
rotation of the forearm (supination), and valgus force (valgus posterolateral). A progressive
circular disruption of the soft tissues occurs, beginning on the lateral side of the elbow.
Posterolateral elbow dislocation also may occur with a combination of axial loading, external
rotation of the forearm, and varus force.
The LCLC is disrupted with all elbow dislocations.Some surgeons believe that the MCL is
always disrupted with elbow dislocation; however, this is controversial.
PLRI and LCLC injury
Trauma (elbow dislocation, fracture-dislocation, subluxation, or sprain)
A fall onto an outstretched hand that supinates the forearm with a valgus thrust and axially
loads the forearm leads to PLRI.
PLRI primarily is an instability pattern of the ulnohumeral articulation, with secondary
involvement of the radiocapitellar joint.
The radioulnar articulation remains stable.
The elbow dislocates because of progressive failure of the LCLs (RCL and LUCL), the
anterior capsule, and possibly the MCL. In many patients, the common extensor origin is
avulsed proximally from the lateral epicondyle. Occasionally, ligamentous disruption results
from supinator crest avulsion or impaction fractures of the capitellum.4,11
LCL disrupted in almost all patients with an elbow fracture-dislocation12
Common extensor/supinator 66% of patients
MCL: 50% of elbow fracture-dislocations

Sprains: hyperextension with or without varus stress
Recurrent PLRI of the elbow develops in only a small number of patients with an elbow
dislocation. Most patients are successfully treated via brief immobilization and early
protected range of motion (ROM).
Studies show decreased healing potential of the LCL, analogous to lateral knee
ligamentous structures.11,13,16
Chronic attenuation or attritional injury
Cubitus varus deformity
Acquired: supracondylar fracture malunion
Congenital
Tardy posterolateral elbow instability is a potential late complication of a varus
supracondylar humerus malunion.
In tardy posterolateral elbow instability, the abnormal lateral thrust across the joint line
caused by the malunion slowly stretches the LUCL over time.1
Varus alignment (25° or 20° with lateral joint opening on varus stress) results in
contracture of the triceps, which alters the triceps vector medially to further accentuate
deformity.
Lateral epicondylitis
Historically, chronic crutch users (paraplegic patients, polio)
Iatrogenic injury
Inadvertent sectioning during surgical management/arthroscopy
Repeated steroid injections
Varus posteromedial instability (VPMI)
Mechanism and pattern of injury
VPMI may occur after a fall onto an outstretched hand that applies a varus thrust to the
elbow.
A combined sagittal coronoid medial facet fracture and a LUCL injury are the essential
lesions.
The instability occurs as the distal humerus subluxates into the proximal ulnar lesion. If this
occurs, the proximal ulna rotates in a posterior and varus direction, producing
incongruency.
On the lateral aspect of the elbow, traction tears the lateral ligaments, usually without bony
injury.

Classification
Acute Dislocation
Elbow dislocations are classified according to whether they are simple or complex and the
direction of displacement.
Simple versus complex dislocation
Simple: dislocation without osseous injury
Complex: dislocation with osseous injury
Terrible triad injury: characterized by an elbow dislocation with an LCLC tear, a radial head
fracture, and a coronoid fracture
Varus posteromedial rotatory instability: characterized by an LCL tear with a fracture of the
medial facet of the coronoid or a comminuted coronoid fracture
Direction of displacement (position of the distal fragment relative to the proximal fragment)
Posterior dislocations are most common. They may occur in the following directions:
Posterior
Posterolateral
Posteromedial (Figure 1).
Anterior, medial, lateral, and divergent dislocations also can occur.

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Pain: primarily lateral elbow pain, over the origin/insertion of the LUCL
Subjective instability
Mechanical symptoms
Often with elbow extension (rising from a chair or getting out of bed)
Catching or locking more often reported than recurrent dislocations
Patient history includes the following:
Elbow trauma
Supracondylar humerus/distal humerus fractures
Prior elbow arthroscopy, open procedures (Kocher approach)
Recurrent dislocations
Lateral epicondylitis (with or without surgical management or steroid injections)

Physical Examination
Acute Dislocation
Neurovascular status should be documented (before and after elbow reduction).
Open injuries and compartment syndrome, which require immediate surgical management,
should be ruled out.
Posterolateral Rotatory Instability
Detailed inspection of the elbow and contralateral elbow for deformity, alignment, and surgical
scars
ROM, varus/valgus stress examination with special attention to apprehension or guarding,
mechanical symptoms and subluxation
Physical examination tests attempt to re-create the mechanism of injury of forearm supination
and elbow extension against axial loading.
Application of varus torsion during physical examination may help detect subtle instability.17
The most common provocative physical examination tests (improved accuracy if performed
under anesthesia) performed to detect PLRI include the following:
Posterolateral pivot-shift test
Arm overhead in shoulder internal rotation
Valgus stress, axial compression, hypersupination, at 20° of flexion
Positive test: subluxation of the elbow/radial head with clunk and shift, with flexion
coinciding with reduction of the elbow joint
Radial head posterolateral drawer test
Arm overhead, shoulder in internal rotation
Forced supination at 45° of flexion
Positive test: posterolateral subluxation of the elbow or apprehension
Push-up/chair-rise test
Forearms in supination and abduction of shoulder
Positive: reluctance to extend the elbow past approximately 40° of flexion or subluxation.
Improvement in symptoms if anteromedial support to the radial head with the thumb to
prevent subluxation
Apprehension/pain with varus stress
Varus Posteromedial Instability

Physical examination—Decreased ROM; painful arc of motion; and, occasionally crepitus, are
noted on physical examination.
Accuracy/Precision of Physical Examination
Physical examination is clinically valuable; however, a paucity of data exists regarding the
sensitivity and specificity of provocative maneuvers.18
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Acute Dislocation
Plain AP and lateral radiographs of the elbow are necessary to document congruent reduction.
Oblique radiographs may be useful to identify periarticular fractures.
Posterolateral Rotatory Instability
Plain radiographs (AP/lateral view of elbow, with or without oblique view)
Acute dislocation: frank posterolateral subluxation
Varus stress radiographs
Full supination with varus loading
A 2-mm lateral joint opening indicates LCLC injury.
PLRI
Lateral radiographs with forced supination and valgus stress may be most useful.19
Positive test with radioulnar posterior subluxation, widening of the ulnohumeral joint, and
radiocapitellar disassociation
In purely ligamentous PLRI or LCLC injury, radiographs may be negative; however, associated
lesions of the radial head, capitellum, coronoid, and articular surface may be observed.
Varus Posteromedial Instability
With VPMI, AP radiographs will demonstrate loss of articular congruency of the medial joint
line and/or a sagittal coronoid fracture. Opening of the radiocapitellar articulation is common,
indicating injury to the lateral ligaments.

9/24

Radial head fractures are not observed in patients with this injury pattern. This distinguishes
VPMI from terrible triad injury.
Computed Tomography
Acute Dislocation
CT is useful to identify associated osseous injury.
With an incongruous reduction, CT or MRI should be considered to identify potential
incarcerated osteocartilaginous fragments.
Posterolateral Rotatory Instability
May help characterize concomitant fractures of the radial head, ulna, medial/lateral
epicondyles, capitellum, or coronoid.
Varus Posteromedial Instability
CT is the best imaging modality to define the orientation and size of the coronoid fracture.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Acute Dislocation
With incongruous reduction, CT or MRI should be considered to identify potential incarcerated
osteocartilaginous fragments.
Posterolateral Rotatory Instability
MRI is unreliable to assess the integrity of the LUCL because of the oblique course of the
ligament; considerable false-negative rate.4,20
May be useful for surgical planning13
Requires thin cuts to accurately section the ligament.21
Cartilaginous injury may be appreciated on magnetic resonance arthrograms.
Positive findings include attenuation or disruption of the posterior fibers of LUCL.
Diagnosis


Diagnosis
Because of the large differential diagnoses for lateral elbow pain, varus and posterior
rotatory instability occasionally are misdiagnosed as the more common lateral
epicondylitis. Although both disease processes may present as lateral elbow pain and
tenderness, they can be differentiated via a careful patient history, provocative
maneuvers on physical examination (chair apprehension, push-up apprehension, pivot-
shift test, and posterolateral rotatory drawer test), dynamic imaging studies, and
advanced imaging studies.
Differential Diagnosis
Lateral epicondylitis
Posterolateral (humeroradial synovial) plica syndrome
Radial nerve entrapment
Articular arthrosis and associated loose bodies
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Techniques/Procedures
Acute Injuries
Reduction of the joint under adequate analgesia is performed first.
Reduction maneuver for posterior dislocations—Controlled reduction is performed by
applying in-line traction, progressive elbow flexion, and anterior directed force to the
olecranon.
Post-reduction stability is assessed.
In posterior dislocations, the elbow typically is more unstable in extension. Therefore, the
elbow should be immobilized in 90° of flexion. Under the same anesthetic event used for
initial reduction, an examination under anesthesia may be useful to document the degree of
extension at which subluxation begins to occur; this may guide the degree to which
extension should be blocked during early ROM.

11/24

If the LCL is disrupted and the MCL is intact, the elbow will be more stable with the forearm in
pronation.
If the LCL and the MCL are disrupted, the forearm should be immobilized in neutral because of
loading of the medial tissues.
A posterior splint is applied. Typically, the forearm is placed in a splint for 5 to 7 days, with the
elbow positioned at 90° and with appropriate forearm rotation.
Post-reduction radiographic assessment (AP and lateral views with the elbow at 90° and
appropriate forearm rotation) is performed to confirm concentric reduction. Attention is
directed to ensuring concentric ulnohumeral reduction and alignment of the radial head with
the capitellum. If the articulation appears incongruent, CT may be considered to assess for
entrapped fragments. after reduction is confirmed, the arm is immobilized for 5 to 7 days.
Depending on stability, the splint can be removed to allow for early active ROM exercises with
the use of a brace, with or without an extension block as dictated by the extension block splint.
Early ROM: full prono-supination from 90° to full flexion
Progressive extension of 30° weekly or more, depending on the examination under
anesthesia; forearm in pronation or neutral depending on the pattern of instability.
6 weeks: full supination in extension
Activity modifications, avoiding gravity varus, bracing, and strengthening of the extensors may
decrease symptoms in milder or chronic cases.
Surgical Management
Indications
Acute Dislocation
Indications
Stability of the elbow cannot be achieved via reduction and immobilization
Osteochondral fragment or soft-tissue entrapment prevents concentric reduction
Complex dislocation: associated fractures
Open injuries
Neurovascular injuries requiring surgical management
Relative indication: reducible joint that is unstable (dislocates) with the elbow extended
between 90° and 60°.
Acute LCL Injury or Other Bony Injury Requiring Surgical Fixation

Midsubstance tear
Chronic LCLC Insufficiency
Recurrent dislocation or pain
Contraindications
Acute Dislocation
Patients with severe medical comorbidities
Procedure
Surgical Approaches
Skin incision and approach depend on concomitant pathology, most commonly via Kocher
approach (Figure 2)
Interval: intermuscular plane (anconeus and extensor carpi ulnaris) identified by fat raphe
Incise the fascia from distal to proximal to center over the lateral epicondyle.
Full-thickness capsular flaps: graft to run over closed capsule (Video 1)
Figure 2 Intraoperative photographs show the standard Kocher approach to the elbow. A,
Photograph shows the landmarks and incision. L = lateral epicondyle, RH = radial head, SR =
supracondylar ridge, UC = ulnar crest. B, Photograph shows the interval between the anconeus
(A) and the extensor carpi ulnaris (E). C, Photograph shows that after the interval is opened, the
torn lateral collateral ligament (L) and the annular ligament (AL) can be visualized. (Reproduced
from Carpenter SR, Sathyendra VM, Murthi AM: Elbow rehabilitation after lateral collateral
ligament reconstruction, in Green A, Hayda R, Hecht AC, eds: Postoperative Orthopaedic
Rehabilitation. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2018, pp 149-156.)

Technique
Acute dislocation
Surgical procedures
The incision can be made in the posterior midline or on the lateral elbow over the Kocher
interval (extensor carpi ulnaris and anconeus) with or without a medial approach.
Open reduction of the elbow with repair (or reconstruction) of the LCLC is performed;
stability is then assessed.
Hinged or static external fixation is required only if the elbow is unstable after other
surgical procedures have failed to result in maintained concentric, stable reduction.
Acute LCLC injury
Primary repair with the use of two strands of heavy, nonabsorbable suture through the
midsubstance of LCLC to the lateral epicondyle at the isometric point (geometric enter of
capitellum)
One strand each along the anterior and posterior halves of fibers in a running, locking
fashion
Augment by passing through the superficial common extensor or supinator fibers

Passed through anterior and posteriorly, aiming bone tunnels at isometric point
Suture anchor as secondary option
If the elbow remains unstable, the MCL may need to be addressed (direct repair or
reconstruction); stability is then assessed again.
Chronic LCLC injury
For grossly unstable elbows and elbows in which nonsurgical management fails, LUCL or
LCLC reconstruction with the use of a graft is indicated.22
Direct repair is associated with inferior outcomes.4,23,24
Graft material may be autograft or allograft. Palmaris longus,plantaris, gracilis, lateral triceps
fascia, or other common tendon graft material may be used (Figure 3).
Ulnar tunnel steps
Kocher approach, with full-thickness capsular flaps (as for an acute LCLC injury)
Ulnar tunnel—Identify the supinator crest via palpation.
First hole: posterior to the tubercle of the supinator crest
Second hole: 1 to 1.5 cm proximal and posterior to the first hole
Use a curet to connect the holes and create the tunnel.
Avoid dorsal tunnel placement, which may lead to iatrogenic fracture.

open docking technique. A, The graft is passed through a tunnel created at the crista supinatoris.
B, The posterior limb is passed through the isometric point at the lateral epicondyle. C, The

Humeral fixation steps
Goal: isometric tension throughout flexion-extension arc (Figure 4)
Identify isometric point at the geometric center of the capitellum, confirm via suture
through the ulnar tunnel, held over the proposed point and by bringing the elbow through
flexion-extension arc. Correct point will result in no change in tension on suture.
First hole: slightly proximal and posterior to isometric point, anterior to the lateral
humeral column
Second hole: directly posterior to isometric point, posterior to the lateral humeral column
Third hole: isometric point
Graft docked with anterior and posterior strands from the ulnar tunnels, both passed
through isometric point (third hole)25

Longer strand to pass through the tunnel out hole (first hole), over bone and in through the

Remaining graft length incorporated and sutured to ulnar strands
This technique allows for differential tensioning of the anterior and posterior strands of the

Alternatively, a one-hole technique has been described, with both strands of grafts placed
through a single tunnel originating at isometric point and aimed posterior to the lateral
humeral column ridge.
With either technique, the graft should be tensioned with the joint reduced, the forearm in
full pronation, and the elbow at 45° flexion.
Close the capsule under the graft, if possible, to allow the graft to remain extra-articular.
Radial head repair/replacement should be performed in patients with a concomitant
fracture.
Coronoid fractures with instability also should be reduced and fixed to restore ulnohumeral
joint stability.

VPMI
Early recognition of the instability pattern and management is necessary to avoid rapid onset
of posttraumatic arthritis.
Management of VPMI consists of repair of the LCL and restoration of the proximal ulnar joint
surface and/or open reduction and internal fixation of the coronoid fracture.
Anteromedial coronoid fractures that are small, minimally displaced, and demonstrate no
evidence of elbow subluxation may be managed nonsurgically.
Outcomes are improved via anatomic reduction and secure coronoid fixation. Varus
malalignment of the anteromedial facet or varus subluxation of the elbow leads to arthritic
changes and poor functional results.
Postoperative Management
Acute dislocation
Depending on postoperative stability of the elbow, active ROM exercises may begin with the
use of a brace with or without an extension block. The extension block may be decreased
gradually or removed at approximately 2 to 3 weeks, with a goal of full active extension by
approximately 6 to 8 weeks postinjury. Active ROM exercises are performed through the
stable arc motion, maintaining the most stable position of the forearm through the arc of
motion. Active pronation and supination with the elbow at 90° are initiated as soon as the
splint is removed (5 to 7 days postinjury) to prevent rotational contracture.
LCL injury or reconstruction
Immobilization for 2 to 3 weeks postoperatively
90° of flexion, forearm pronation
Early ROM in pronation, with no extension past 30° of flexion
Active ROM can be initiated 6 weeks postoperatively.
Patient should be educated on techniques to protect the repair/reconstruction from
natural gravity varus during activities of daily living by pronating the arm and avoiding
overhead activities in supination, which strain the graft and repair site.26
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Acute dislocation
SEND FEEDBACK

AAOS | Elbow Instability: Lateral Collateral Ligament Complex Insufficiency

18/24

The most common pitfall is failure to attain and maintain concentric reduction after surgical
or nonsurgical management. The joint must be reduced concentrically, and management
does not stop until satisfactory reduction is achieved.
Forearm rotation is used to its fullest advantage to attain or maintain concentric reduction.
Early active ROM through a stable arc with the use of splints may help prevent contracture.
If open reduction is required, a stepwise surgical approach should be followed.
Complications
Acute Dislocation
Loss of extension (most common)
Early active ROM exercises may help prevent or minimize occurrence.
Static, progressive splinting may be initiated if the elbow is less inflamed (typically, 6 to 8
weeks postinjury).
Neurovascular injuries
Compartment syndrome
Articular surface injuries
Chronic or recurrent elbow instability; residual laxity is common with stress radiographs;
however, recurrent instability is observed in less than 10% to 20% of patients.
Late osteoarthritis
Heterotopic ossification
Posterolateral Rotatory Instability
Recurrent instability: 3% to 8% incidence
Infection: open injury or postoperative
Nerve injury: posterior interosseous or superficial radial nerve
Elbow stiffness
Outcomes
Recurrent instability after repair or reconstruction is not uncommon (as high as 25%).13
Acute repair
Superior outcomes with primary repair of acute injuries versus reconstruction13
Augmented repair technique via suture augmentation construct is effective.21,27

Reconstruction
Good outcomes at midterm follow-up with excellent function for ligamentous
allografts/autografts and tendon allograft repairs.6,14,28
Some studies show better subjective patient-reported outcomes versus ligament repair in
those with chronic injuries.23,24
Superior outcomes compared with arthroscopic plication or electrothermal shrinkage29
91% and 87% revision-free survival of reconstruction at 2 and 6 years postoperatively,
respectively
Early outcomes with complete LCLC versus LUCL-only reconstruction are associated with
similar Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand and Mayo Elbow Performance Index
scores for all etiologies of PLRI.30
Reconstruction with radial head replacement
Poor outcomes if concomitant pathology not addressed
Mark as Complete
